title: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
description: Grade 6 Science: nutrients (carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins, minerals), the balanced diet, food tests and deficiency diseases — notes, examples and a test.

topics.title: Essential Nutrients (Carbohydrates, Fats, Proteins, Vitamins, Minerals)
topics.concept:
The food we eat is made of useful substances called nutrients. Different foods contain different nutrients, which is why we need to eat a variety of food. There are five main nutrients, plus water and roughage.

  • Carbohydrates — the body’s main source of energy. Found in rice, wheat, bread, potato and sugar. We test for starch (a carbohydrate) using iodine solution, which turns blue-black.
  • Fats — give more energy than carbohydrates and help store it; they also keep the body warm. Found in ghee, oil, butter and nuts. A food with fat leaves an oily patch on paper that lets light through.
  • Proteins — the body-building nutrients, needed for growth and repair. Found in dal, beans, paneer, eggs, fish and milk. A protein test using copper sulphate and caustic soda turns the food violet.
  • Vitamins and minerals — needed in small amounts to protect the body and keep it working well (more on these later in this chapter).

Foods that mainly give energy (carbohydrates and fats) are called energy-giving foods; proteins are body-building foods; and vitamins and minerals are protective foods.

examples.problem: Example 1: A few drops of iodine solution are put on a slice of potato and it turns blue-black. What does this tell you?
examples.solution:
Iodine solution is the test for starch, a carbohydrate.

  • A blue-black colour means starch is present.
  • So the potato contains carbohydrate (starch).
examples.answer: The potato contains starch (a carbohydrate), shown by the blue-black colour with iodine.

examples.problem: Example 2: Ravi is recovering from an illness and his body needs to repair itself and grow. Which nutrient should his meals be rich in, and name two foods that provide it.
examples.solution:
Growth and repair of the body are the work of proteins.

  • His meals should be rich in proteins.
  • Good sources include dal, beans, paneer, eggs, fish or milk.
examples.answer: Proteins — from foods such as dal, paneer, eggs, fish or milk.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why do mountaineers and people in very cold places eat plenty of fatty foods?
examples.solution:
Fats give a lot of energy and help keep the body warm.

  • In the cold the body uses more energy to stay warm.
  • Fatty foods provide that extra energy and warmth.
examples.answer: Because fats give a large amount of energy and help keep the body warm in the cold.

recap:
• Carbohydrates and fats are energy-giving foods; fats give more energy and warmth.
  • Proteins are body-building foods, needed for growth and repair.
  • Vitamins and minerals are protective foods, needed in small amounts.
  • Tests: iodine → blue-black for starch; oily patch on paper for fat; violet colour for protein.

quiz.q: Iodine solution is used to test for:
quiz.explanation: Iodine turns blue-black in the presence of starch, a carbohydrate.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is mainly needed for the growth and repair of the body?
quiz.explanation: Proteins are the body-building nutrients used for growth and repair.

topics.title: Concept of a Balanced Diet
topics.concept:
A balanced diet is a diet that contains all the nutrients — carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins and minerals — along with roughage and water, in the right amounts for a person’s needs.

No single food has every nutrient, so a balanced diet is built by combining foods. A simple Indian thali — roti or rice, dal, vegetables, curd and a little salad — is a good example, because together these foods supply energy, body-building and protective nutrients.

The right amount of food is not the same for everyone. A growing child, a labourer doing heavy work and an office worker all need different amounts. Eating far more energy-food than the body uses is stored as fat and can lead to being overweight; eating too little leaves a person weak and undernourished.

  • Roughage (dietary fibre) comes from vegetables, fruits and whole grains. It has no nutrient value but adds bulk and helps the body get rid of waste, preventing constipation.
  • Water helps digest food, carries nutrients and wastes in the blood, and controls body temperature. We get it by drinking and from foods such as fruits.

examples.problem: Example 1: A lunch of only plain white rice is not a balanced meal. Suggest two things to add to make it balanced, and say which nutrients they provide.
examples.solution:
Rice gives mainly carbohydrate; a balanced meal needs body-building and protective foods too.

  • Add dal — provides protein (body-building).
  • Add vegetables/salad — provide vitamins, minerals and roughage (protective).
examples.answer: Add dal (protein) and vegetables or salad (vitamins, minerals and roughage) to balance the carbohydrate-rich rice.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why does roughage form an important part of our diet even though it provides no nutrients?
examples.solution:
Roughage helps the working of the digestive system.

  • It adds bulk to food.
  • It helps move waste through the body and prevents constipation.
examples.answer: Roughage adds bulk and helps the body remove waste, preventing constipation, even though it gives no nutrients.

examples.problem: Example 3: Two children eat the same number of meals, but one is very active in sports and the other is not. Why might the active child need to eat more?
examples.solution:
The body needs more energy food when it does more physical work.

  • Active muscles use up more energy.
  • So the active child needs more energy-giving food to meet that need.
examples.answer: Because the active child uses more energy in sport, so they need more energy-giving food than the less active child.

recap:
• A balanced diet has all five nutrients plus roughage and water, in the right amounts.
  • No single food is complete, so we combine foods (e.g. a thali).
  • The right amount differs with age and activity; too much energy-food causes weight gain, too little causes weakness.
  • Roughage aids digestion and prevents constipation; water helps digestion, transport and temperature control.

quiz.q: A balanced diet is one that:
options: Has all nutrients, roughage and water in the right amounts
Is the same for every person
quiz.explanation: A balanced diet supplies every nutrient, plus roughage and water, in amounts suited to the person.

quiz.q: Roughage is important in our diet because it:
quiz.explanation: Roughage adds bulk and helps the body get rid of waste, preventing constipation.

topics.title: Deficiency Diseases and Prevention
topics.concept:
When a person’s food lacks a particular nutrient for a long time, they may fall ill. A disease caused by the long-term shortage of a nutrient is called a deficiency disease. These are prevented simply by eating a balanced diet that includes the missing nutrient.

Many deficiency diseases are caused by a lack of particular vitamins or minerals:

  • Vitamin A — protects eyesight and skin. Shortage causes poor vision, especially night blindness. Sources: carrots, papaya, mango, green leafy vegetables, milk.
  • Vitamin C — keeps gums and skin healthy and helps fight illness. Shortage causes scurvy (bleeding, swollen gums). Sources: amla, oranges, lemons, guava, tomatoes.
  • Vitamin D — helps the body use calcium for bones. Shortage causes rickets (weak, bent bones). Sources: sunlight, milk, eggs.
  • Calcium (mineral) — builds strong bones and teeth. Shortage causes weak bones and teeth. Sources: milk, curd, green leafy vegetables.
  • Iron (mineral) — needed to make healthy blood. Shortage causes anaemia (weakness, tiredness). Sources: green leafy vegetables, jaggery, dates.
  • Iodine (mineral) — shortage causes goitre (swelling of the neck). Source: iodised salt.

Eating a variety of fresh fruits and vegetables every day is the best way to prevent these diseases.

examples.problem: Example 1: A child finds it hard to see in dim light at night. Which vitamin is likely missing, and which foods would help?
examples.solution:
Difficulty seeing in dim light is night blindness, linked to vitamin A.

  • The child likely lacks vitamin A.
  • Foods that help: carrots, papaya, mango, green leafy vegetables and milk.
examples.answer: Vitamin A — provided by carrots, papaya, mango, green vegetables and milk.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why is iodised salt recommended for cooking?
examples.solution:
Iodised salt supplies the mineral iodine.

  • A long-term lack of iodine causes goitre, a swelling of the neck.
  • Using iodised salt prevents iodine deficiency.
examples.answer: It supplies iodine, preventing the deficiency disease goitre (swelling of the neck).

examples.problem: Example 3: A person feels weak and tired and is found to have too little healthy blood (anaemia). Which mineral is deficient, and name two foods to add.
examples.solution:
Healthy blood needs the mineral iron.

  • Anaemia is caused by a lack of iron.
  • Iron-rich foods: green leafy vegetables, jaggery or dates.
examples.answer: Iron — add iron-rich foods such as green leafy vegetables, jaggery or dates.

recap:
• A deficiency disease is caused by a long-term lack of a nutrient and is prevented by a balanced diet.
  • Vitamin A → night blindness; Vitamin C → scurvy; Vitamin D → rickets.
  • Calcium → weak bones/teeth; Iron → anaemia; Iodine → goitre.
  • Eating a variety of fresh fruits and vegetables daily prevents most deficiency diseases.

quiz.q: Scurvy, which causes bleeding and swollen gums, is caused by a lack of:
quiz.explanation: Vitamin C keeps gums and skin healthy; its shortage causes scurvy.

quiz.q: A long-term shortage of iron in the diet leads to:
quiz.explanation: Iron is needed to make healthy blood; its lack causes anaemia.

questions.q: The useful substances present in food are called:
questions.explanation: Nutrients are the useful substances in food.

questions.q: The main energy-giving nutrient in rice and wheat is:
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates are the body’s main source of energy.

questions.q: Which nutrient gives the most energy and helps keep the body warm?
questions.explanation: Fats give more energy than carbohydrates and help keep the body warm.

questions.q: Body-building foods are rich in:
questions.explanation: Proteins are needed for the growth and repair of the body.

questions.q: Iodine solution turns blue-black when added to a food. This shows the food contains:
questions.explanation: Iodine is the test for starch, a carbohydrate.

questions.q: An oily patch left on paper that lets light through shows the presence of:
questions.explanation: Fats leave a translucent oily patch on paper.

questions.q: Vitamins and minerals are called protective foods because they:
options: Keep the body healthy and fight disease
questions.explanation: Vitamins and minerals protect the body and keep it working well.

questions.q: A balanced diet is one that contains:
options: All nutrients, roughage and water in the right amounts
questions.explanation: A balanced diet supplies every nutrient plus roughage and water in suitable amounts.

questions.q: Roughage in our food mainly helps to:
questions.explanation: Roughage adds bulk and helps the body get rid of waste.

questions.q: Night blindness is caused by the deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Vitamin A protects eyesight; its shortage causes night blindness.

questions.q: Rickets, which causes weak and bent bones, is due to a lack of:
questions.explanation: Vitamin D helps the body use calcium for bones; its shortage causes rickets.

questions.q: Which mineral is needed to make healthy blood?
questions.explanation: Iron is required for healthy blood; its lack causes anaemia.

questions.q: Goitre, a swelling of the neck, is prevented by using:
questions.explanation: Iodised salt supplies iodine, preventing goitre.

questions.q: Which food group does a thali (roti, dal, vegetables, curd) best represent?
questions.explanation: A thali combines energy, body-building and protective foods, making a balanced meal.

questions.q: Eating far more energy-rich food than the body needs can lead to:
questions.explanation: Extra energy food is stored as fat and can make a person overweight.

questions.q: Two foods are tested. Food X turns iodine blue-black; food Y turns violet in the protein test. Which is correct?
options: X has starch and Y has protein
X has protein and Y has fat
questions.explanation: Blue-black with iodine means starch (X); violet in the protein test means protein (Y).

questions.q: A diet rich in rice, sugar and ghee but with no dal, milk, fruits or vegetables would most likely cause poor:
questions.explanation: Such a diet lacks proteins (growth) and vitamins/minerals (protection).

questions.q: Why are fruits and vegetables especially important even though they give little energy?
options: They supply vitamins, minerals and roughage
questions.explanation: Fruits and vegetables are the chief source of protective vitamins, minerals and roughage.

questions.q: A villager regularly eats green leafy vegetables and jaggery. Which deficiency disease are they LEAST likely to get?
questions.explanation: Green leafy vegetables and jaggery are rich in iron, which prevents anaemia.

questions.q: Sunlight helps prevent rickets because it helps the body make:
questions.explanation: Sunlight helps the body make vitamin D, which is needed for strong bones.

questions.q: An athlete and an office worker eat the same balanced foods. The athlete should mainly increase the amount of:
questions.explanation: More physical activity uses more energy, so the athlete needs more energy-giving food.
